title: Valid Anagram
description: Brute force to optimized: sorting both strings versus counting letter frequencies in one pass.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement
Problem Summary: Given two strings s and t, return true if t is an anagram of s, meaning it uses exactly the same letters the same number of times, just rearranged.

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem
Given two strings s and t, return true if t is an anagram of s, meaning it uses exactly the same letters the same number of times, just rearranged.

blocks.title: Analogy: Rearranging the Same Set of Scrabble Tiles
blocks.text: Like checking whether two words could have been formed from the exact same bag of Scrabble tiles. If both words use identical letters in identical quantities, one is simply a rearrangement of the other.

blocks.caption: Two strings are anagrams when every letter appears the same number of times in both

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: s = "anagram", t = "nagaram"

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Every letter in s appears the same number of times in t","a: 3 in both, n: 1 in both, g: 1 in both, r: 1 in both, m: 1 in both","both strings are built from the exact same 7 letters, just in a different order"],["Answer","true","every letter count matches exactly"]]}

blocks.text: Example: s = "rat", t = "car"

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["t contains a \"c\" that s does not have at all","the letter counts cannot match","s has no c to account for the one appearing in t"],["Answer","false","a mismatched letter count immediately rules out an anagram"]]}

blocks.text: Edge case: s and t have different lengths
If the two strings are not even the same length, they cannot possibly use the same letters the same number of times, so the answer is immediately false without checking anything else.
5. How Should We Think?
It helps to ask exactly what property makes two strings anagrams, and how much of that property really needs checking.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Sorting both strings and comparing them works, since two true anagrams always sort into the identical sequence, but sorting rearranges far more information than the question actually asks about.

Observation 2: Contains Duplicate and Subarray Sum Equals K already showed that a hash map tallying occurrences turns a comparison problem into simple counting, with no ordering step required at all.

Observation 3: Here that idea extends naturally to two strings: tally every letter of s once, then walk through t subtracting one from each letter's count as it is consumed, only order within each string is irrelevant, the counts are everything.

Observation 4: If t ever asks for a letter that is not available (its count is already 0 or never existed), the strings cannot be anagrams, and if every count lands back at exactly 0 after t is fully consumed, they are proven to match exactly, confirmed by tracing s equal to "anagram" and t equal to "nagaram" through to true.
Recognizing that only the letter counts matter, not the full ordering, is what replaces an O(n log n) sort with a single O(n) counting pass.
6. Brute Force Solution
Sort both strings into alphabetical order. If they are true anagrams, sorting will rearrange them into an identical sequence of characters.
Step by step algorithm

items: If the two strings have different lengths, return false immediately.
Sort both strings.
Compare the sorted strings directly for equality.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The length check runs first since it is a cheap way to reject the overwhelming majority of non anagram pairs immediately.
Sorting brings every true anagram pair to an identical character sequence, since sorting only depends on which characters are present and how many of each, never their original order.
A direct equality check on the sorted results is sufficient once both are sorted, since any letter count mismatch would have produced different sorted sequences.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Two strings are anagrams exactly when sorting brings them to the same sequence of characters, so this correctly detects every true anagram pair.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log n), dominated by sorting both strings.
Space: O(n) or O(log n) depending on the sort implementation.
Limitation: sorting does more work than necessary. Checking whether two strings are anagrams only requires knowing whether their letter counts match, not their exact rearranged order.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the brute force works but is wasteful: sorting establishes a full, exact ordering for both strings, when the question only ever cares about how many times each letter appears, never their order.

What direct counting fixes: tallying every letter of one string once, then subtracting those same counts while scanning the other, checks exactly the property the problem asks about, nothing more.

What a count reaching zero prematurely, or a missing letter, reveals: an immediate proof that the two strings cannot be anagrams, without needing to finish scanning.

The core idea: count once, subtract once, and let every count landing back at exactly zero be the proof of a true anagram.

Count how many times each letter appears in s, then walk through t subtracting one from each letter's count as it is seen. If the two strings are true anagrams, every count lands back at exactly zero once t has been fully processed.
9. Optimized Solution
Count every letter in s, then subtract letter counts while scanning t.
Dry run for s = "anagram", t = "nagaram"

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result"],"rows":[["Count letters in s","a:3, n:1, g:1, r:1, m:1"],["Subtract each letter of t as it is scanned","every count returns to 0 by the end"],["All counts are zero","true anagram"]]}

blocks.caption: Optimized: count letters in one string, subtract while scanning the other

blocks.text: Why This Works

This works because the count map after tallying s holds the exact multiset of letters s is built from, and subtracting one for every letter t consumes can only reach exactly zero across the board if t consumes precisely that same multiset, no more of any letter and no less.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What Happens","Result"],"rows":[["A letter in t is missing from the count map, or its count has already reached zero","The function returns false immediately","A letter t needs but s does not have enough of correctly rules out an anagram"],["Every letter of t is successfully subtracted without ever hitting a missing count","The function reaches the end and returns true","Every letter of s was matched exactly once by a corresponding letter in t"]]}

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), one pass over each string.
Space: O(1), since the alphabet size is fixed regardless of the string length.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways
This is the standard character frequency counting pattern, and its O(n) time is already optimal since every character of both strings must be examined at least once to be certain no mismatch exists.
Common Mistakes

items: Forgetting the length check up front, which is a cheap way to reject many non anagrams immediately.
Using a full hash map when the problem guarantees only lowercase English letters, where a fixed size array of 26 counters is simpler and faster.

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["Two empty strings","Trivially anagrams of each other."],["Strings containing Unicode characters","May need a hash map instead of a fixed size array if the alphabet is not guaranteed to be simple lowercase letters."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tips
Mention both the sorting approach and the counting approach, and explain that counting wins because it avoids the log factor that sorting introduces.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid sorting", think: count letters in one string, subtract while scanning the other.
If the interviewer says "what if the alphabet is not just lowercase letters", think: swap the fixed size array for a hash map, the logic stays identical.
If the interviewer says "can you check this without extra space", think: sorting in place still costs O(n log n) time, so there is a genuine time versus space tradeoff to discuss.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: Why is the length check performed before any counting begins?
How would this approach change if the strings could contain any Unicode character, not just lowercase English letters?
How would you check whether one string is an anagram of any substring of another, longer string?
How would you group a whole list of strings into sets of anagrams of each other?
How would you adapt this approach to check if two strings become anagrams after removing exactly one character from each?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Contains Duplicate and Subarray Sum Equals K, whose hash based counting is the direct ancestor of tallying letters here.
Group Anagrams, which extends this exact counting idea to bucket many strings together by their shared letter signature.
Any "do these two collections contain the same elements" question, where counting occurrences is almost always cheaper than sorting or pairwise comparison.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Brute force: O(n log n) time, O(n) or O(log n) space. Optimized: O(n) time, O(1) space.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: character frequency counting, tallying one string and subtracting while scanning the other.
Core Idea: two strings are anagrams exactly when their letter counts match exactly, so tallying one and subtracting while scanning the other proves or disproves that in a single pass.
Time: O(n log n) for the brute force, O(n) for the optimized approach.
Space: O(n) or O(log n) for the brute force's sort, O(1) for the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: anagram checking only depends on letter counts, never on order, so any technique that establishes a full ordering, like sorting, does strictly more work than necessary.
Interview Difficulty: both approaches are simple to state; picking counting over sorting, and explaining exactly why, is the small but telling detail.
One line memory trick: count up one string, count down the other, every count should land on zero.
